"'''Sledgehammer'''" is a song by the English [[Rock music|rock]] musician [[Peter Gabriel]]. It was released in April 1986 as the lead single from his fifth studio album, ''[[So (album)|So]]'' (1986).<ref>{{cite web|title= Sledgehammer |website= Petergabriel.com |access-date= 29 April 2020 |url= https://petergabriel.com/release/sledgehammer/}}</ref> It was produced by Gabriel and [[Daniel Lanois]]. It reached No. 1 in Canada on 21 July 1986, and remained there for four weeks; No. 1 on the [[Billboard Hot 100|''Billboard'' Hot 100]] chart in the United States on 26 July 1986;{{sfn|Dean|2003|p=160}} and No. 4 on the [[UK Singles Chart]], thanks in part to its music video, which was directed by [[Stephen R. Johnson]]. It was his biggest hit in North America and ties with "[[Games Without Frontiers (song)|Games Without Frontiers]]" as his biggest hit in the United Kingdom.

The song's video won a record nine [[MTV Video Music Awards]] at the [[1987 MTV Video Music Awards]]<ref name="MTV">{{cite web|title= VIDEO MUSIC AWARDS – Biggest Winners |publisher= [[MTV]] |access-date= January 18, 2015 |url= http://www.mtv.com/ontv/vma/archive/multiple-winners.jhtml|archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20130825125309/http://www.mtv.com/ontv/vma/archive/multiple-winners.jhtml|url-status= dead|archive-date= August 25, 2013}}</ref> and Best British Video at the 1987 [[Brit Awards]].<ref name="Time">{{cite magazine|title= Peter Gabriel, 'Sledgehammer' (1986) |magazine= [[Time (magazine)|Time]] |date= 28 July 2011 |url= http://www.time.com/time/specials/packages/article/0,28804,2085389_2085392_2085368,00.html |url-status= dead |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20120228125440/http://www.time.com/time/specials/packages/article/0,28804,2085389_2085392_2085368,00.html |archive-date= 28 February 2012}}</ref><ref name="Brits">{{cite web |title= The BRITs 1987 |publisher= [[Brit Awards]] |date= 9 February 1987 |access-date= 19 November 2011 |url= http://www.brits.co.uk/history/shows/1987 |archive-date= 17 March 2014 |archive-url= https://archive.today/20140317150236/http://www.brits.co.uk/history/shows/1987 |url-status= dead }}</ref> The song also saw Gabriel nominated for three [[29th Annual Grammy Awards|Grammy Awards]] for [[Grammy Award for Best Male Rock Vocal Performance|Best Male Rock Vocal Performance]], [[Grammy Award for Record of the Year|Record of the Year]] and [[Grammy Award for Song of the Year|Song of the Year]].<ref name="Grammys">{{cite web|title= 29th Grammy Awards – 1987 |website= Rock on the Net |access-date= 19 November 2011 |url= http://www.rockonthenet.com/archive/1987/grammys.htm}}</ref> In a 2005 poll conducted by [[Channel 4]], the music video was ranked second on their list of the [[100 Greatest (TV series)|100 Greatest Pop Videos]].<ref>{{cite web|title= 100 Greatest ... (The 100 Greatest Pop Videos) |publisher= [[ITN Source]] |access-date= 31 May 2019 |url= http://www.itnsource.com/en/shotlist/ITVProgs/2005/02/06/Y09420007/ |url-status= dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150221233131/http://www.itnsource.com/en/shotlist/ITVProgs/2005/02/06/Y09420007/ |archive-date= 21 February 2015}}</ref>

==Background==
"Sledgehammer" was initially written during the [[Birdy (Peter Gabriel album)|''Birdy'']] sessions in 1984. A version was recorded featuring bassist [[Leland Sklar]] and drummer [[Chester Thompson]], but Gabriel was not satisfied with it.<ref>{{Cite AV media |url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0FuxB3o_1x4 |title=1119. Peter Gabriel |date=11 October 2022 |last=Leland Sklar |access-date=2026-04-13 |via=YouTube}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |date=19 May 2017|title=Katche talks about groove-writing tips {{!}} My Drum Lessons |url=https://mydrumlessons.co.uk/2017/05/manu-katche-session-drummer-reflects-on-his-career/ |access-date=2026-04-13 |website=My Drum Lessons}}</ref> Thus, in Spring 1985,<ref name="SOS" /> he revisited the song and recorded another version with his full backing band, including [[David Rhodes (guitarist)|David Rhodes]], [[Tony Levin]] and drummer [[Manu Katché]].<ref name=":0">{{Cite magazine |last=Fisher |first=Connie |date=December 1987 |title=Manu Katché |magazine=[[Modern Drummer]] |page=56 |issue=98}}</ref> Gabriel presented the song just as they were packing up their equipment after initial sessions, citing his original intention to include the song on his next album after ''So''.{{sfn|Scott|2012|loc=17:38}} [[Manu Katché]] was preparing to board a taxi and return home to Paris when Gabriel coaxed him into recording "Sledgehammer".{{sfn|Scarfe|2021|pp=47-48}}<ref name="Google">{{cite AV media |people=[[Google]]; Gabriel, Peter |title=Peter Gabriel: "Back to Front", Talks at Google |date=22 October 2012 |medium=Interview |url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=xPL7cebKI5o  |archive-url=https://ghostarchive.org/varchive/youtube/20211222/xPL7cebKI5o |archive-date=22 December 2021 |url-status=live|access-date=8 April 2025}}{{cbignore}}</ref>{{Reference page|location=6:35–7:01}} The song was recorded live in two or three takes with the full band playing and Gabriel on keyboards and vocals.<ref name=":0" /><ref>{{Cite web |last=Ernould |first=Franck |date=November 2005 |title=Manu Katché: Session Drumming & Music Technology |url=https://www.soundonsound.com/people/manu-katche |access-date=14 April 2026 |website=www.soundonsound.com}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Daly |first=Andrew |date=9 April 2026 |title=“It was a very conscious decision on Peter’s part to come up with material that would make a very good and accessible record”: Guitarist David Rhodes on the making of Peter Gabriel’s chart-smashing classic So |url=https://www.guitarworld.com/artists/guitarists/david-rhodes-on-the-making-of-peter-gabriel-so |access-date=14 April 2026 |website=Guitar World |language=en}}</ref> [[Tony Levin]] opted to record his part on a [[fretless bass]] with a [[plectrum|pick]] and through an octave pedal.{{sfn|Scott|2012|loc=21:41}}

Gabriel noted that he was influenced by soul music when writing "Sledgehammer" and also considered recording a soul-oriented album with a mixture of covers and original compositions.{{blockquote|As a teenager, soul music was one of the things that made me want to be a musician. It was really passionate and exciting... [[Wayne Jackson (musician)|Wayne Jackson]], who plays on that track, was also with [[Otis Redding]] and was touring with him when I saw them in London. So that was a thrill for me, just to get a whole lot of fan stories. But I think the song was more influenced by many of those [[Stax Records|Stax]] and [[Atlantic Records|Atlantic]] tracks rather than Otis particularly."|Peter Gabriel, July 1986<ref name="WMMR">[[WMMR]] interview, 16 July 1986, as transcribed by Fred Tomsett in Gabriel [[fanzine]] ''White Shadow'' #2, circa 1989</ref>}}

Gabriel contacted Jackson to assemble a horn section that included Jackson on trumpet, [[Mark Rivera]] on saxophone, and Don Mikkelsen on trombone.<ref name="Experiencing">{{Cite book |last=Bowman |first=Durrell |title=Experiencing Peter Gabriel: A Listener's Companion |date=2 September 2016 |publisher=Rowman & Littlefield |isbn=9781442252004 |location=Lanham, Maryland |pages=127–131}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last=Easlea |first=Daryl |title=Without Frontiers: The Life and Music of Peter Gabriel |publisher=[[Omnibus Press]] |year=2014 |isbn=978-1-4683-0964-5 |location=London, UK |page=249}}</ref> Gabriel explained that he wanted a real horn section on "Sledgehammer" to capture some of the intricacies of brass playing that could not be achieved with a synthesiser. He cited the slow brass swells in the second verse as an example of the expressiveness that he desired.<ref name="Hammond">{{cite magazine|first=Ray |last= Hammond |title=Peter Gabriel – Behind the Mask |magazine=[[Sound on Sound]] |via= Mu:zines |date=January 1987 |access-date=16 December 2024 |url=https://www.muzines.co.uk/articles/peter-gabriel-behind-the-mask/1494 |issue=Jan 1987 |pages=40–44}}</ref> The song also features a [[Synthesizer|synthesised]] ''[[shakuhachi]]'' flute generated by an [[E-mu Systems]] synthesizer and resampled and layered with other sounds from the [[Fairlight CMI]].<ref name="SOS"/> Gabriel said that the "cheap organ sound" came from an expensive [[Prophet-5]] synth, which he regarded as "an old warhorse" sound tool.<ref name="Hammond"/> The backing vocals were sung by [[P. P. Arnold]], Coral "Chyna Whyne" Gordon, and Dee Lewis, who also did the backing for "[[Big Time (Peter Gabriel song)|Big Time]]".<ref name="Experiencing"/> Overdubs for the horn section and backing vocals took place in September 1985 at [[Power Station (recording studio)|Power Station Studios]] in New York City.<ref name="Experiencing"/><ref name="SOS">{{cite web|title=Classic Tracks: Peter Gabriel 'Sledgehammer' |first=Richard |last=Buskin |website=soundonsound.com |url=https://www.soundonsound.com/techniques/classic-tracks-peter-gabriel-sledgehammer |date=August 2014 |access-date=June 16, 2025}}</ref>

==Release==
Gabriel pushed for "Sledgehammer" to be the first single from ''So'' because he considered it to be different from the rest of the album. When discussing the decision to release "Sledgehammer" as the album's first single, Gabriel said that "I think it was a surprise for people who have a fixed image of what I am and what I do."<ref name="Hammond"/>

All editions of the single included the track "Don't Break This Rhythm", whereas the [[twelve-inch single]] was appended with an "'85 Remix" of 1982's "[[I Have the Touch]]" as its B-side.{{sfn|Scarfe|2021|p=133}}<ref>{{Cite magazine |date=12 April 1986 |title=New Product |url=https://www.worldradiohistory.com/UK/Music-Week/1986/Music-Week-1986-04-12.pdf |access-date=5 April 2026 |magazine=[[Music Week]] |page=3 |via=World Radio History}}</ref> US versions of the single also contained an extended dance [[remix]] of "Sledgehammer".{{sfn|Scarfe|2021|p=133}}

"Sledgehammer" is Gabriel's only No. 1 hit on the US ''Billboard'' Hot 100. It replaced "[[Invisible Touch (song)|Invisible Touch]]" by his former band [[Genesis (band)|Genesis]]; coincidentally, that group's only US No. 1.  Genesis lead singer [[Phil Collins]] later jested about the occurrence in a 2014 interview, stating, "I read recently that Peter Gabriel knocked us off the No. 1 spot with 'Sledgehammer'. We weren't aware of that at the time. If we had been, we'd probably have sent him a [[telegram]] saying: 'Congratulations – bastard.{{'"}}<ref name=guardian>{{cite web |url = https://www.theguardian.com/culture/2014/oct/14/how-we-made-invisible-touch-phil-collins-mike-rutherford-genesis |title = Phil Collins and Mike Rutherford: how we made Invisible Touch |last = Barnett |first = Laura |date= 14 October 2014 |website = [[The Guardian]] | access-date = 8 July 2022}}</ref>

"Sledgehammer" also achieved success on other ''[[Billboard (magazine)|Billboard]]'' charts in 1986, spanning the [[Mainstream Rock (chart)|Album Rock Tracks]] (two weeks at the summit in May and June)<ref>{{cite book|first= Joel |last= Whitburn |author-link= Joel Whitburn |year= 2004 |title= The Billboard Book of Top 40 Hits |edition= 8th |publisher= Billboard Publications |page= 246}}</ref> and [[Dance Club Songs|Hot Dance Club Play]] (one week atop this chart in July).<ref>{{cite book|first= Joel |last= Whitburn |year= 2004 |title= Hot Dance/Disco 1974–2003 |publisher= Record Research Inc. |page= 106}}</ref> In the UK, the single peaked at number four, tying it with 1980's "[[Games Without Frontiers (song)|Games Without Frontiers]]"⁠ as his highest-charting song in that country.<ref>{{Cite web |title=PETER GABRIEL |url=https://www.officialcharts.com/artist/16171/peter-gabriel/ |access-date=1 November 2024 |website=Official Charts |language=en}}</ref>

==Critical reception==
"Sledgehammer" has been described as [[dance-rock]],<ref>{{cite magazine|first= Terry |last= Staunton |title= Peter Gabriel: So |page= 103 |magazine= [[Classic Rock (magazine)|Classic Rock]] |issue= 178 |date= December 2012}}</ref> [[funk rock]],<ref>{{cite news|first= Mac |last= Randall |title= Gabriel, Beck and Miller Struggle with Gravity |newspaper= [[The New York Observer]] |date= 10 July 2002 |access-date= 2 May 2022 |url= http://observer.com/2002/10/gabriel-beck-and-miller-struggle-with-gravity/}}</ref> [[soul music|soul]],<ref>{{cite magazine|first= Steve |last= Pond |title= Peter Gabriel Hits the Big Time |magazine= [[Rolling Stone]] |date= 29 January 1987 |access-date= 2 May 2022 |url= https://www.rollingstone.com/music/music-news/peter-gabriel-hits-the-big-time-106473/}}</ref> and [[New wave music|new wave]],<ref>{{cite web|url=https://ultimateclassicrock.com/new-wave-songs/|title=Top 50 New Wave Songs|first=Michael|last=Gallucci|date=November 7, 2024|website=Ultimate Classic Rock|access-date=November 8, 2024}}</ref> Ryan Reed of ''[[Paste (magazine)|Paste]]'' called the song a danceable "[[blue-eyed soul]]-strut".<ref>{{cite magazine|first= Ryan |last= Reed |title= Peter Gabriel: The Darwin of Pop |magazine= [[Paste (magazine)|Paste]] |date= 13 October 2011 |access-date= 2 May 2022 |url= http://www.pastemagazine.com/articles/2011/10/peter-gabriel-the-darwin-of-pop.html |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20141006131414/http://www.pastemagazine.com/articles/2011/10/peter-gabriel-the-darwin-of-pop.html |archive-date= 6 October 2014}}</ref> ''[[Billboard (magazine)|Billboard]]'' said that the song possessed a "straightforward r&b sound, almost as direct as its [[Stax Records|Stax/Volt]] ancestors."<ref>{{Cite magazine |date=10 May 1986 |title=Singles |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=8CQEAAAAMBAJ& |access-date=5 April 2026 |magazine=[[Billboard (magazine)|Billboard]] |page=79 |via=Google Books}}</ref> ''[[Cashbox (magazine)|Cashbox]]'' called it a "riveting, hard-hitting track" that evoked the work of [[Steve Winwood]]. They also called the song a continuation of Gabriel's "innovative work" that manifested in "imaginative [and] creative results".<ref>{{Cite magazine |date=10 May 1986 |title=Single Releases |url=https://www.worldradiohistory.com/Archive-All-Music/Cash-Box/80s/1986/CB-1986-05-10.pdf#page=11 |access-date=5 April 2026 |magazine=[[Cashbox (magazine)|Cashbox]] |page=11 |via=World Radio History}}</ref> ''[[Music & Media]]'' said that the song showcased Gabriel "in his most soulful mood ever."<ref>{{Cite magazine |date=3 May 1986 |title=Singles Guide |url=https://www.worldradiohistory.com/UK/Music-and-Media/80s/1986/M&M-1986-05-03.pdf |access-date=5 April 2026 |magazine=[[Music & Media]] |volume=3 |issue=17 |page=9 |via=World Radio History}}</ref>

''[[Trouser Press]]'' gave it as an example of Gabriel's "characteristically sophisticated music" which in this case "touches on [[funk]]".<ref>{{cite magazine|first1= Steven |last1= Grant |first2= Ira |last2= Robbins |title= Peter Gabriel |magazine= [[Trouser Press]] |access-date= 4 October 2014 |url= https://www.trouserpress.com/entry.php?a=peter_gabriel}}</ref> Stewart Mason of [[AllMusic]] thought that "Sledgehammer"{{'s}} "earthier foundation keeps the song from getting distracted from the pounding, swaggering groove at its core", adding that "it's not his masterpiece, but it's probably his best pop song. Later attempts at rewriting it, like 1992's dismal '[[Steam (Peter Gabriel song)|Steam]]', didn't work half as well."<ref>{{Cite web |last=Mason |first=Stewart|title=Sledgehammer - Peter Gabriel|website=AllMusic |url=https://www.allmusic.com/song/sledgehammer-mt0045458919 |access-date=9 February 2024 |language=en}}</ref>

==Music video==
The "Sledgehammer" [[music video]] was commissioned by [[Tessa Watts]] at [[Virgin Records]], directed by [[Stephen R. Johnson]] and produced by Adam Whittaker. [[Aardman Animations]] and the [[Brothers Quay]] provided [[Clay animation|claymation]], [[pixilation]], and [[stop motion]] animation that gave life to images in the song.<ref name="Cavalier">{{cite web |last1=Cavalier |first1=Stephen |title=100 Greatest Animated Shorts / Sledgehammer / Stephen R. Johnson |url=https://www.skwigly.co.uk/100-greatest-animated-shorts-sledgehammer/ |website=Skwigly: Online Animation Magazine |date=24 September 2015 |access-date=1 September 2023}}</ref> Johnson and Gabriel wanted the music video to be satisfying on repeat viewings and set out to accomplish this by incorporating multiple ideas that were both "inventive and funny".<ref name="Angelic">{{Cite web |last=McIver |first=Joel |date=22 October 2007 |title=Angelic Gabriel |magazine=[[Record Collector]] |url=https://recordcollectormag.com/articles/angelic-gabriel |access-date=26 March 2025}}</ref> They spent a couple of weeks generating ideas  and later invited Brothers Quay and Aardman Animations to develop the music video.<ref name="Google"/>{{Reference page|location=7:27–7:59}}

Gabriel said that the music video was shot frame by frame. For one scene, Gabriel lay under a sheet of glass for 16 hours with raw fish.<ref>{{cite book|first= Alan |last= Cross |title= The Impact of the Music Video |date= 7 October 2001 |publisher= [[Corus Entertainment|Corus Radio]]}}</ref><ref name="Google"/>{{Reference page|location=8:10–8:41}} "It took a lot of hard work," Gabriel recalled. "I was thinking at the time, 'If anyone wants to try and copy this video, good luck to them.{{'"}}<ref name="WMMR"/> For each frame of a ten-second sequence, clouds were painted across Gabriel's face to create the illusion of moving clouds.<ref name="Hammond"/>

Two dead, headless, featherless chickens were animated using stop motion and shown dancing along to the synthesised ''[[shakuhachi]]'' solo. This section was animated by [[Nick Park]], of Aardman Animations, who was refining his work in plasticine animation at the time and later created ''[[Wallace & Gromit]]''.{{sfn|Scott|2012|loc=27:05}}<ref name="Google"/>{{Reference page|location=7:01–7:23}} The video ended with a large group of extras jerkily rotating around Gabriel, among them his daughters Anna-Marie and Melanie, the animators themselves and director Stephen Johnson's girlfriend. A total of 100 hours were spent shooting the music video, with each second of video consisting of 25 unique poses from Gabriel.<ref name="Gallo">{{Cite book |last=Gallo |first=Armando|title=Peter Gabriel |publisher=SonicBond |year=1986 |isbn=0-7119-0783-8 |location=United Kingdom |page=90}}</ref>

A major hit on music television, "Sledgehammer" won nine [[MTV Video Music Awards]] in 1987,<ref name="MTV"/> the [[MTV Video Music Award#Most wins for a single video|most awards a single video has won]].<ref name="Time"/> It ranked at number four on [[MTV]]'s ''100 Greatest Music Videos Ever Made'' (1999). "Sledgehammer" has also been declared MTV's number one animated video of all time.<ref>{{cite web|title= Episode Guide – Transcript of MTV's "Top 10 Animated Videos Countdown" |website= Outpost Daria |date= 28 June 1998 |url= http://www.outpost-daria.com/ts_top10.html |archive-date= 10 July 2012 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20120710053630/http://www.outpost-daria.com/ts_top10.html}}</ref> The video was voted number seven on [[The Music Factory|TMF]]'s ''Ultimate 50 Videos You Must See'', which first aired 24 June 2006. It ranked at number 2 on VH1's "Top 20 Videos of the '80s" and number one on "Amazing Moment in Music" on the Australian TV show ''[[20 to One|20 to 1]]'' in 2007. It won Best British Video at the 1987 [[Brit Awards]] and was nominated for the Best Music Video category for the first annual [[Soul Train Music Awards]] in that same year.{{cn|date=September 2025}}

According to ''[[Time (magazine)|Time]]'' magazine, "Sledgehammer"{{'s}} music video is the all-time most played music video on MTV.<ref>{{cite magazine | url=https://entertainment.time.com/2011/07/28/the-30-all-time-best-music-videos/slide/peter-gabriel-sledgehammer-1986/ | title=Peter Gabriel, 'Sledgehammer' (1986) | magazine=[[Time (magazine)|Time]] | date=26 July 2011 | last1=Levy | first1=Glen }}</ref> Gabriel recalled that the video was broadcast in the Soviet Union, India, and China, which had otherwise refrained from playing his other material.<ref name="Angelic"/>

The music video was [[remaster]]ed into [[4K resolution]], and was released in 2018 through [[Apple Music]].<ref>{{cite web|first= Buddy |last= Iahn |title= Peter Gabriel 'Sledgehammer' video remastered in 4K |website= The Music Universe |date= 21 July 2018 |access-date= 6 September 2021 |url= https://themusicuniverse.com/peter-gabriel-sledgehammer-video-remastered-in-4k/ |url-status= live |archive-date= 28 August 2021 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20210828195708/https://themusicuniverse.com/peter-gabriel-sledgehammer-video-remastered-in-4k/}}</ref>

==Live performances==
Gabriel first performed "Sledgehammer" on his 1986-1987 [[This Way Up Tour]]. [[Akai]] [[sampler (instrument)|samplers]] were used to pull the horn parts from the studio recording that were played by the Memphis Horns. The sounds were placed onto floppy discs and loaded into a keyboard played by [[David Sancious]], who would then assign the parts to different notes of the instrument. He mentioned that he used "four different horn parts and different slides and punctuations", which were then spread across the keyboard. Sancious also used a keyboard to trigger the sound of [[shakuhachi]] flute and organ on this tour.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Wiser |first=Carl |date=15 February 2021 |title=David Sancious : Songwriter Interviews |url=https://www.songfacts.com/blog/interviews/david-sancious |access-date=26 April 2026|website=[[Songfacts]]}}</ref> He later included the song on his [[Secret World Tour]].<ref>{{cite web |url=https://chicagoreader.com/music/peter-gabriels-performance-art-rock/ |title=Peter Gabriel's performance art rock |last=Keough |first=Kevin |date=15 July 1993 |website=[[Chicago Reader]] |access-date=27 April 2026}}</ref>

extract:
"Sledgehammer" is a song by the English rock musician Peter Gabriel. It was released in April 1986 as the lead single from his fifth studio album, So (1986). It was produced by Gabriel and Daniel Lanois. It reached No. 1 in Canada on 21 July 1986, and remained there for four weeks; No. 1 on the Billboard Hot 100 chart in the United States on 26 July 1986; and No. 4 on the UK Singles Chart, thanks in part to its music video, which was directed by Stephen R. Johnson. It was his biggest hit in North America and ties with "Games Without Frontiers" as his biggest hit in the United Kingdom.
The song's video won a record nine MTV Video Music Awards at the 1987 MTV Video Music Awards and Best British Video at the 1987 Brit Awards. The song also saw Gabriel nominated for three Grammy Awards for Best Male Rock Vocal Performance, Record of the Year and Song of the Year. In a 2005 poll conducted by Channel 4, the music video was ranked second on their list of the 100 Greatest Pop Videos.
